ThemeName: Locomotion suitability was conditional on spatial scale and task context
Definition: Distance, environmental geometry, and task purpose redistributed practical fit; no method was universally optimal.
Scope: All methods; Precision and Navigation tasks; application preferences
ContradictoryOrDivergentCases: Baseline could be inefficient at long range; Tsunami and Minimap were not preferred for every short-range or geometry-constrained task.
RelatedQuantitativeFindings: Route time, teleport count, path efficiency, method-by-route interaction

ThemeName: Spatial awareness depended on what the technique kept perceptually available
Definition: Incremental movement, map abstraction, and destination preview exposed different spatial information and supported orientation through different mechanisms.
Scope: All methods, principally the Navigation task
ContradictoryOrDivergentCases: Minimap sometimes supplied a useful global overview; Tsunami did not always support orientation when landmarks or destinations were difficult to see; repeated Baseline jumps could also disrupt orientation.
RelatedQuantitativeFindings: Spatial-awareness composite, environmental continuity, phase-specific yaw/pitch, latency and head rotation

ThemeName: Observed usability reflected the locomotion concept, interaction mapping, and implementation
Definition: Experience arose at concept, controller-mapping, and implementation/UI levels; prototype limitations were not treated as inherent technique limitations.
Scope: All methods; Precision and Navigation tasks; tutorial feedback
ContradictoryOrDivergentCases: Positive and negative precision experiences occurred under all methods; some causal attributions could not be assigned confidently to implementation-specific causes.
RelatedQuantitativeFindings: Direct-hit precision, sequential first-landing error and corrective teleportations

ThemeName: Practical adoption depended on learnability, coherence, and demonstrated utility
Definition: Familiarity, acclimatization, coherence, appeal, and task utility jointly shaped willingness to use a method; novelty alone was insufficient.
Scope: Tutorial, both tasks, overall preference and application use
ContradictoryOrDivergentCases: Not every participant adapted or preferred a novel technique; speed, workload, usability, comfort, fun, and preference did not rank methods identically.
RelatedQuantitativeFindings: Within-method adaptation, net/total time, RAW-TLX, usability, preference, CSQ-VR
